results.title: Ecological Model Uncertainty → Term
results.content: It is an inherent part of working with complex systems and should be incorporated into how we use ecological models for environmental decision-making Meaning → Environmental Decision-Making represents the systematic process of selecting a course of action from various alternatives, considering the potential environmental impacts and aiming for sustainable outcomes. Building upon the foundational understanding of Ecological Model Uncertainty, we now move into a more detailed examination of its sources, types, and implications. Ecological Model Uncertainty Meaning → Model uncertainty, in the context of sustainability, refers to the recognition that predictions and assessments of environmental, social, and economic systems are inherently limited by incomplete knowledge and simplified representations. Understanding these sources is the initial step toward mitigating their impact and improving model robustness: Types of Ecological Model Uncertainty Beyond the sources, Ecological Model Uncertainty can be categorized into different types, each with distinct implications for model interpretation and use: Acknowledging and quantifying these various forms of uncertainty is not a sign of model failure, but rather a hallmark of rigorous and responsible ecological modeling. By recognizing the sources and types of Ecological Model Uncertainty, experts can move beyond simplistic interpretations of model outputs and engage in more nuanced and effective environmental decision-making. The next step is to explore methods for quantifying, managing, and communicating this inherent uncertainty in ecological models. At an academic level, Ecological Model Uncertainty transcends a mere acknowledgment of imprecision; it becomes a central epistemological and methodological consideration in ecological research and environmental governance. Ecological Model Uncertainty, in its academic context, is not merely a statistical artifact, but a fundamental characteristic of our attempts to represent and predict complex natural systems, demanding sophisticated methodologies and philosophical reflection. This perspective acknowledges that ecological systems are characterized by: This redefined understanding of Ecological Model Uncertainty moves beyond a purely technical framing to encompass philosophical dimensions. By embracing Ecological Model Uncertainty as a fundamental characteristic of complex systems, rather than a deficiency to be overcome, we can cultivate a more robust, adaptive, and ultimately more sustainable relationship with the natural world.

results.title: Overview of Least Cost Path Analysis - Geography Realm
results.content: # Overview of Least Cost Path Analysis. Least cost path analysis is a distance analysis tool within GIS that uses the least cost path or the path between two locations that costs the least to those travelling along it to determine the most cost-effective route between a source and destination. When using least cost path analysis in GIS, the eight neighbors of a raster cell are evaluated and the generated path moves to the cells with the smallest accumulated or cost value (“Distance Analysis Using ArcGIS”). Least cost path analysis is an important GIS tool to understand because it has many different applications – all of which can help businesses, city planners and other users save time and money. ## **Requirements for Least Cost Path Analysis**. The cost distance measure portion of least cost path analysis is centered on the node-link raster cell representation (Chang). An algorithm is an important component of least cost path analysis because accumulative cost between two cells can be calculated by adding the costs of connecting the two cells but least accumulative costs are challenging because there are many different ways to connect two cells and they do not have to be immediate neighbors (Chang). ## **Creating a Least Cost Path Analysis**. Once the four requirements for conducting a least cost path analysis are met it is important to consider and correctly weight the rasters making up the cost raster to create an effective least cost path analysis (“Creating the Least Cost Path.”). The first step in the least cost path analysis workflow is to reclassify the value ranges of the rasters to make sure that they use a common weighting scale. The final step in conducting a least cost path analysis is to use the cost distance and cost direction rasters as the main inputs in the cost path tool. ## **Applications/Examples of Least Cost Path Analysis**. Least cost path analysis has a number of different GIS applications. Whatever its use, least cost path analysis is an important tool in GIS because it has the ability to help businesses, city planners and other users save time and money.

results.title: Solved: Cutting rasters to precise extent and cell size - Esri Community
results.content:
Title: Solved: Cutting rasters to precise extent and cell size - Esri Community
# Cutting rasters to precise extent and cell size. I want to clip all four rasters such that the output will have the same # of rows/columns, X&Y cell size, and extent. The issue is with the SOILS raster, which regardless of whether I use Extract By Mask, Clip, or Data Extraction the output raster will differ in number of columns/rows, X&Y cell size, or extent. It is imperative that all four rasters match precisely in extent, cell size, and columns/rows in order for me to use the data with MaxEnt. I've attached screencap of an excel showing the rows/columns, cell size (x & y), and extent for the different data layers. If needed I resample all these smaller data layers with the appropriate cell size (that of DEM raster). I next cut the resampled data layers using "extract by mask" using the DEM raster layer as the mask, and under Environment | Processing Extent | Snap to Raster = DEM raster. This produces raster output that is precisely the same extent and cell size. *Tools that honor the Snap Raster environment will adjust the extent of output rasters so that they match the cell alignment of the specified snap raster.*. The cell Size (Y), and extent (Top & Right) differ from the DEM raster even when using Snap Raster set to the DEM raster. Thanks for the insight Dan. I've noticed that most tools that allow you to specify cell size apply the provided cell size to both X and Y, and the X and Y of most of my raster data differ between X and Y. I also ensured that the cell size (both X and Y) were square and the same for all the raster layers. Eachof the rasters output shared identical extent, rows/columns and cell size which was desirable. I then converted my USGS/NCRS Soils shape file  (containing ~25,000 polygons) to a raster using the cell size of the other raster files (slope, dem, and aspect). Here is a screen cap showng the two polygon shape files (rectangleboundary & kyboundary) which were used to cut the soils\_rectangle2 and DEM raster layers from the even larger extent source data.
